# Translation

Kesh counted the steps down to the Eighth Forge the way he counted everything: under his breath, without thinking, a habit older than his apprenticeship. Forty-one steps. Two hundred six strikes on the grinding wheel before the first bell. Four days until his journeyman examination.

The coal chute had been filled last night. He noticed, because on delivery mornings the yard always looked poorer—the coal pile sinking lower, the mountain swallowing more of the sky. Four baskets of coal this week already. Two, last quarter.

He wrote his name on the day's work order, claimed the first wheel slot, and let the wheel decide the shape of his morning. Six years had taught his hands to read steel through leather. Six years had left scars, some still fresh enough to itch. The blade under his fingertips was honest—metal always was: it either held an edge or it didn't, and no ledger under heaven could change that.

"Seventy-one," he said. "Seventy-two."

"Talk while you grind and you'll ruin the bevel." Oren Vael stood in the doorway of the assembly room, the day's invoices clipped to a slate. Fifty-seven years old, and he still stood like a man leaning into wind, feet planted wide, weight forward. For three years he had left the first wheel slot to Kesh every morning, whether there was work or not. Everyone on Farlow's lower terrace said Master Vael was a generous man. "Shoulder passes are always seventy. You know that number better than I do."

"The coal came early," Kesh said. His eyes never left the wheel. "Fourth basket this week. Twice the quarterly draw."

"Yes."

"And the output sheet doesn't show double. I checked Sunday. Twenty-two finished blades, eleven repairs. Same as autumn."

Oren looked at the coal chute, then at Kesh, and named a price. "Coal in Farlow is up nine coppers a cart since the canal froze. Merchants on the east steps are hoarding. Men who buy before the peak pay more and call it foresight." He clipped the slate to his belt. "Your examination is Thursday. The wheel is forty paces to your left."

Kesh went back to the wheel. Seventy passes at the shoulder on the first blade, seventy on the second, thinking about nine coppers a cart. Foresighted men bought coal. Men with reasons bought double the amount and said nothing about it.

The debt collectors had already come twice this month. His mother had met the second visit with her mending money, telling the man through the closed door that her son was nearly made journeyman, and journeymen earned full wages. The man said that by his reckoning winter began the Thursday after next. The house was collateral. The house had been collateral since the year the guild refused to pay a single copper for his father's death—because the contract had been bought and sold twice before the collapse, and whoever held it last owed nothing to anyone beneath it. Kesh had been thirteen that year. He remembered the price of everything from that year and had forgotten almost everything else.

Mid-morning, the dock wagon came. That was ordinary; the Eighth Forge shipped to the east docks every ten days, mostly plow fittings, cheap work nobody in the city coveted. Kesh helped load, because carrying counted on the examination sheet, and that sheet was an entire week.

The crates were wrong.

They came down from the assembly room already packed, which was itself unusual. Oren always built his own crates and stenciled them himself with the guild template—VIII-F, every time. These crates were marked before Kesh ever saw them. He lifted the first into the wagon bed and the weight reached him before his arms did. Forty pounds heavier than plow fittings. He set the crate down and read the seal.

IX-M.

The Ninth Forge's mark, the M-suffix for military contract work, stamped in black on one crate after another. Six crates. The Eighth Forge had never once shipped for the Ninth. The Ninth Forge had run all winter on two apprentices and a dying fire—the whole terrace knew it. The Ninth couldn't fill a single saber contract, let alone boxes this heavy.

"Plow fittings run heavy these days," Kesh said.

"They're not plow fittings." Oren carried out the last crate himself, one-armed against his hip, sliding it into the bed without a sound. "The Ninth mixed up their orders. Their wagon can't make the dock ramp in this weather, so ours goes down instead. Ordinary freight. Freight's paid by the run anyway." He slapped the crate lid the way he slapped finished work. "Twelve coppers a run east. Good money for a morning."

"Whose contract?"

Oren was counting something on his slate. Then he said: "Your left glove's leaking blood. Change the wrapping before you go back on the wheel, or the examination board will smell it on you." He turned and went inside.

At noon the wagon pulled out with six crates, and Kesh could see no bill of lading anywhere on it. Oren walked the driver to the head of the steps, said a few words too low to carry, and came back alone.

Kesh spent the afternoon on the eleven farm-blade repairs, and he kept counting, because when his mind had nowhere to go, it only counted. Eleven blades at market price: thirty-one coppers. The coal those eleven blades burned, by his own forge's reckoning: nine coppers. Two hundred six strikes a blade, forty-one steps, twelve coppers a run. The coal ledger had doubled. The shipments had not. The Eighth Forge was buying fire it never sold, hauling crates heavy as rifles and stamped with another forge's name.

He wanted to ask. He had a question ready made, and it was a good one, and he honed it in his head all afternoon: the Ninth Forge's order book was a public record at the guild hall, and it would show which contract the IX-M crates belonged to. If it showed nothing, then Oren was stamping his own forge's mark onto military freight for a man with no paperwork at all. That was the work that ends with a rope. Guild wars grew fat on exactly such men.

And Thursday's examination was written in Oren Vael's hand. Kesh needed the journeyman's mark, needed full wages, needed eleven months of pay to clear his mother's debt before the collectors settled accounts for winter. One question asked in the wrong tone, and the wheel slot could go to Tavin Rul—the one who never spoke to anyone about anything. In a third-rate guild, loyalty was the whole purse. Everyone knew what became of apprentices who counted other people's coal piles.

At dusk he banked the fire, hung up his gloves, and stood a while in the assembly room doorway, the day's invoices still clipped to the slate. Twenty-two blades sold. Thirty-one coppers. Nine coppers of coal, multiplied by two baskets that belonged to no forge of his. If just one number would hold still, he could nearly balance the ledger in his head—but it wouldn't, and that was the outline of the thing he could not yet see.

Oren was at the far workbench, his back turned, chalk in hand, writing something on the shadowed side of the quench barrel where the lamplight didn't reach.

Kesh looked at the guild hall door—the one he could still reach before it closed tonight—then at his master's back, counting under his breath, one, two, three.

He did not go.
